newsitem.title: USA: US T-bond may rally on Fed rate hike-fund managers.
newsitem.headline: US T-bond may rally on Fed rate hike-fund managers.

text.p: A well-choreographed tightening of U.S. monetary policy combined with mounds of idle cash could spark a rally in the bond market next week, portfolio managers said.

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan once again pointed to the central bank's need to preemptively strike at inflation during testimony before Congress on Thursday, raising expectations that a tightening of monetary policy was likely at the FOMC's meeting next Tuesday.

"If I and the majority of other managers I talk to are correct, the market is likely to rally," said Patrick Retzer, portfolio manager at Heartland Advisers with some $300 million of fixed-income securities under management. "The Fed has successfully set the stage for a tightening that won't cause a large selloff in the markets by telegraphing its intentions over the past week."
"We like the five- to seven-year area, after that the curve gets a lot flatter," said Retzer. "Five-years is a great inflection point where you get rapid rolldown down the curve."
Margaret Patel, managing director and portfolio manager at Northstar Funds said a hike next week was not a done deal, but noted that bonds have already prepared for the possibility of such a move.

"I still think it's 50-50 whether they tighten or not, but the market has already backed up long rates anyway, so I wouldn't be surprised if the market rallied," she said. "It wouldn't be the first time the market rallied on a tightening."
Patel said that at "7.0-ish" yields at the long end of the market would look attractive to many investors, especially if the Fed were viewed as being proactive on inflation.

"Anecdotally, speaking to portfolio managers it seems most people are a little short on their bogey -- whatever that may be -- on Treasuries for a while now. You could see them come back in as buyers," Patel said.
A bogey is a target for purchasing or selling a security or group of securities. For an investor it may represent locking in a certain yield on a bond.

"Everything is on hold. The market's mesmerized by the FOMC meeting," said Jerry Thunelius, senior portfolio manager for the Dreyfus U.S. Treasury Long Term fund. He also saw the possibility of a rally next week, albeit only near-term.
He said asset allocators could find value with yields above 7.0 percent and noted that Japanese buying of Treasuries had been seen on Wednesday for the first time in a long time.
Thunelius said the back end of the market was the best place to be for those in the camp that the Fed will tighten.

He said it was hard to find value at the front end of the market and inflation-indexed bonds were cheap for those thinking no tightening would occur and expensive for those who thought the Fed would move.

An important thing to examine will be the Fed's statement in the aftermath of a tightening, should one occur, Thunelius said. He manages about $1.5 billion in fixed-income securities, mostly longer term Treasuries.
"If they tighten with a statement that this was just done as an insurance measure, it will good for the market" as further tightenings would not seem a threat, he said.
"But if they tighten with an open-ended or no statement" it might not spark a strong rally because it could be interpreted that the Fed had entered a cycle of tightening, Thunelius said.
Some would argue that tightening should be good for the bond market as it helps to control inflation, but Thunelius disagreed.
"Tightening is never good. People making that argument don't take into account the financing costs and speculative forces in the market," he said. "Leverage drives the Treasury market."
Matthew Greenwald, a portfolio manager at Oppenheimer Capital, said much depends on the extent of any Fed moves.
